options.a: Real estate licensees and brokerage practice under Chapter 475, F.S.
options.b: Mortgage brokers and loan originators licensed under Chapter 494, F.S.
options.c: Title insurance agencies and agents licensed under Chapter 626, F.S.
options.d: Building permits and zoning approvals issued by county planning boards

distractorExplanations.b: Chapter 494 mortgage brokers and loan originators are licensed by the Office of Financial Regulation, not by DBPR/FREC.
distractorExplanations.c: Title insurance agents fall under Chapter 626 and the Department of Financial Services, not FREC's Chapter 475 authority.
distractorExplanations.d: Permits and zoning are local government land-use functions; FREC regulates real estate licensees, not county planning decisions.

options.a: A licensed broker associate who supervises the team
options.b: A licensed broker or owner-developer as permitted
options.c: The title company or attorney handling the closing
options.d: A licensed mortgage broker business under Chapter 494

distractorExplanations.a: A broker associate works under a broker and cannot be the employer of record; sales associates must register under a broker or owner-developer.
distractorExplanations.c: Closing agents do not employ sales associates; Chapter 475 requires the associate to be registered under a broker or owner-developer.
distractorExplanations.d: A Chapter 494 mortgage brokerage is regulated by OFR and cannot hold a real estate sales associate's license; it must be a real estate broker.

options.a: On an annual cycle with 14 hours of continuing education
options.b: Every four years with 28 hours of continuing education
options.c: On a biennial cycle with required continuing education
options.d: Every two years, with no education after initial licensing

distractorExplanations.a: Florida licenses renew every two years, not annually; the 14 CE hours are due each two-year renewal period.
distractorExplanations.b: Doubles the real cycle: Florida renews biennially with 14 CE hours per period, not every four years with 28 hours.
distractorExplanations.d: Gets the two-year cycle right but drops the education requirement; post-licensing and then 14 hours of CE are required.

options.a: Spends escrow funds on personal expenses or office bills
options.b: Keeps up to $1,000 of brokerage funds in a sales escrow account to cover fees
options.c: Deposits escrow funds in an interest-bearing account with written consent
options.d: Mixes trust/escrow funds with personal or brokerage operating funds

distractorExplanations.a: Spending escrow money for the broker's own use is conversion, a separate and more serious violation than commingling.
distractorExplanations.b: Florida rules let a broker keep up to $1,000 of personal funds in a sales escrow account (up to $5,000 in a property management account) to cover service charges, so this is permitted and not commingling.
distractorExplanations.c: An interest-bearing escrow account is allowed when the parties agree in writing; it does not mix trust money with operating funds.

options.a: Brokers must follow authorized settlement procedures rather than deciding the dispute themselves
options.b: Brokers may release the deposit to the party they believe is entitled once 30 days pass
options.c: Brokers must return the deposit to the buyer within 15 business days of conflicting demands
options.d: Sales associates may hold the disputed deposit until the parties sign a mutual release

distractorExplanations.b: The 30 business days is the deadline to start a settlement procedure; it does not let the broker pick the winning party.
distractorExplanations.c: Fifteen business days is the deadline to notify FREC of the dispute, not a rule that the buyer gets the deposit back.
distractorExplanations.d: Sales associates may not hold escrow funds; deposits go to the broker, who must use an authorized settlement procedure.

fl-real-estate-readiness-check-license-l.explanation: Florida has specific escrow dispute settlement procedures; associates don't hold escrow personally. Authorized procedures are mediation, arbitration, litigation, or an escrow disbursement order request; FREC notice is due within 15 business days and a procedure must start within 30 business days.

options.a: Be located in the same county as the broker's primary residence address
options.b: Meet statutory office requirements and registration rules for the brokerage
options.c: Be registered as a branch office only when it has three or more associates
options.d: Be located in a commercially zoned building rather than a residence

distractorExplanations.a: Florida has no rule tying the office to the broker's home county; the office must meet the statutory office and sign requirements.
distractorExplanations.c: Every branch office must be registered with DBPR, whatever its headcount; there is no three-associate threshold.
distractorExplanations.d: A Florida broker office may be in a residence if local zoning allows it; the rule is about office requirements, not commercial zoning.

options.a: A civil fine from HUD under RESPA
options.b: Only a warning letter from the MLS
options.c: Disciplinary action by FREC/DBPR
options.d: A Florida Bar referral for discipline

distractorExplanations.a: RESPA covers settlement-service kickbacks and is enforced federally; false licensee advertising is disciplined by FREC/DBPR.
distractorExplanations.b: MLS rules are private; misleading advertising is a Chapter 475 violation that FREC can discipline beyond any MLS warning.
distractorExplanations.d: The Florida Bar disciplines lawyers, not real estate licensees; FREC/DBPR handles advertising violations by licensees.

options.a: Deliver it to the broker within three business days of receipt
options.b: Deposit it in the broker's escrow account within five business days
options.c: Hold it until the seller accepts, then give it to the broker
options.d: Deliver it to the broker by the end of the next business day

distractorExplanations.a: Three business days is the broker's deadline to deposit funds into escrow; the associate must deliver by the end of the next business day.
distractorExplanations.b: Uses an invented five-day window; the associate delivers to the broker by the end of the next business day and the broker deposits within three.
distractorExplanations.c: The next-business-day delivery rule runs from receipt, not from contract acceptance, so holding the deposit until acceptance is a violation.

options.a: Deliver it to the employing broker within three business days of receipt
options.b: Deliver it to the employing broker by the end of the next business day
options.c: Deposit it with the closing attorney within 10 days after acceptance
options.d: Hold it in the listing file until both parties sign the contract

distractorExplanations.a: Confuses the associate's next-business-day delivery deadline with the broker's three-business-day escrow deposit deadline.
distractorExplanations.c: Associates deliver deposits to their employing broker; a 10-day window and direct delivery to the attorney are not the Florida rule.
distractorExplanations.d: Deposits may not sit in the associate's file; the next-business-day delivery rule runs from receipt, not from signing.

options.a: A citation from the Florida Bar for unauthorized practice of law
options.b: Administrative penalties including fines, suspension, or revocation
options.c: A HUD fine under RESPA Section 8 for unearned referral fees
options.d: Civil penalties imposed by the county property appraiser for false listings

distractorExplanations.a: Unauthorized practice of law is a different issue; deceptive advertising is a Chapter 475 violation disciplined by FREC.
distractorExplanations.c: RESPA Section 8 covers kickbacks and unearned fees, not misleading property advertising by a Florida licensee.
distractorExplanations.d: The property appraiser sets assessed values for taxes and has no disciplinary power over real estate licensees.

options.a: A 14-hour continuing education course must be completed before the first renewal or the license expires
options.b: A post-license course must be completed before the first renewal or the license can become null and void
options.c: A 60-hour post-license course must be completed within six months of licensure or the license is suspended
options.d: A post-license course is optional if the associate completes 14 hours of continuing education each year

distractorExplanations.a: The 14-hour CE requirement applies from the second renewal on; before the first renewal a sales associate needs the 45-hour post-license course.
distractorExplanations.c: Sixty hours is the broker post-license figure, and the deadline is the first renewal, not six months; the result is null and void, not suspension.
distractorExplanations.d: Post-licensing education cannot be replaced by CE; Florida requires it before the first renewal or the license becomes null and void.

options.a: Competent parties, offer and acceptance, legal purpose, and consideration
options.b: Competent parties, offer and acceptance, recording, and title insurance
options.c: Offer and acceptance, consideration, notarization, and an earnest money deposit
options.d: Competent parties, legal purpose, consideration, and a licensed broker

distractorExplanations.b: Recording and title insurance protect the buyer after closing but are not elements needed to form a valid contract.
distractorExplanations.c: Notarization and earnest money are common but not required; consideration can be the exchange of promises.
distractorExplanations.d: A broker is not a contract element; owners can contract directly, and the list drops offer and acceptance.

options.a: A nonrefundable fee the seller keeps once the contract is signed
options.b: A good-faith deposit that may be forfeited or returned per contract terms
options.c: The commission the buyer's broker earns when the contract is signed
options.d: A deposit the lender holds to pay future property taxes and insurance

distractorExplanations.a: Earnest money is not automatically the seller's; it is returned or forfeited according to the contract terms.
distractorExplanations.c: Earnest money is held in escrow and usually credited to the buyer at closing; it is not broker compensation.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes a lender's escrow or impound account for taxes and insurance, not an earnest money deposit.

options.a: The seller's ownership interest that passes to the buyer by recorded deed
options.b: The lender's interest in the property created by a recorded mortgage lien
options.c: A buyer's interest in the property under a valid sales contract before closing
options.d: A tenant's right to possess and use the property during a lease term

distractorExplanations.a: That is legal title, which the seller keeps until the deed is delivered; equitable title arises under the contract.
distractorExplanations.b: A mortgage creates a lien for the lender; it is not the equitable title a buyer gets under a sales contract.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes a leasehold estate, not the buyer's equitable interest under a purchase contract.

options.a: Transfers title with full covenants that defend against all prior owners' claims
options.b: Transfers title with warranties limited to the grantor's own period of ownership
options.c: Transfers title held by a decedent's estate under court-supervised probate sale
options.d: Transfers whatever interest the grantor has, without warranties of title

distractorExplanations.a: That describes a general warranty deed, which gives the strongest warranties; a quitclaim gives none.
distractorExplanations.b: That describes a special warranty deed; a quitclaim makes no warranty even for the grantor's own period.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes a personal representative's deed; a quitclaim is defined by having no title warranties.

options.a: Covered title defects and liens that were unknown/undiscovered
options.b: Physical defects in the home that a buyer's inspection missed
options.c: Title defects created by the owner after the policy date
options.d: Encroachments and liens listed as exceptions in Schedule B

distractorExplanations.b: Title insurance covers title risks, not physical condition; missed physical defects are an inspection or disclosure issue.
distractorExplanations.c: A title policy covers defects existing as of the policy date, not problems the owner creates afterward.
distractorExplanations.d: Items listed as Schedule B exceptions are excluded from coverage, not insured.

fl-real-estate-readiness-check-contracts.explanation: Owner's/lender's title policies insure against title risks, not physical property condition. Coverage is as defined in the policy.

options.a: Recorded in public records to be valid
options.b: In writing and signed to be enforceable
options.c: Notarized and witnessed to be enforceable
options.d: Signed by both brokers to be enforceable

distractorExplanations.a: Recording gives constructive notice to third parties; it is not what the Statute of Frauds requires for enforceability.
distractorExplanations.c: Florida deeds need two witnesses, but a sales contract only needs to be in writing and signed to satisfy the Statute of Frauds.
distractorExplanations.d: The Statute of Frauds requires signature by the party to be charged, not by the brokers in the transaction.

options.a: Lets the buyer cancel for any reason before closing
options.b: Sets the liquidated damages if a party defaults
options.c: Makes the contract dependent on a specified event
options.d: Transfers equitable title once the event occurs

distractorExplanations.a: A contingency is tied to a specified event; a free right to cancel for any reason is not how contingencies work.
distractorExplanations.b: Liquidated damages provisions fix the remedy for default; they do not make performance depend on an event.
distractorExplanations.d: Equitable title passes when a valid contract is signed, not when a contingency is satisfied.

fl-real-estate-readiness-check-contracts.explanation: Contingencies protect parties; if unmet per terms, parties may terminate as specified. Typical examples are financing or inspection contingencies.

options.a: Open, visible possession by the occupant
options.b: Delivering a copy of the deed to the buyer
options.c: Telling the buyer about the lien in person
options.d: Recording documents in the public records

distractorExplanations.a: Possession gives actual (inquiry) notice, while constructive notice comes from recording in the public records.
distractorExplanations.b: Delivery passes title between the parties but does not give notice to the world, which requires recording.
distractorExplanations.c: Telling someone directly is actual notice; constructive notice is the legal presumption created by recording.

options.a: Prohibited by Chapter 475 and grounds for license revocation
options.b: Legal but discouraged due to conflict-of-interest concerns
options.c: Legal only for commercial property sold through a broker
options.d: Legal if the broker's fee is capped at 6% of the price

distractorExplanations.a: Many states ban net listings, but Florida does not; they are legal though discouraged because of the conflict of interest.
distractorExplanations.c: Florida law has no commercial-only limit on net listings; they are legal but discouraged for any property type.
distractorExplanations.d: A net listing has no fixed fee cap; the broker keeps the excess over the net, which is exactly the conflict-of-interest concern.

fl-real-estate-readiness-check-contracts.explanation: Florida allows net listings but they create conflicts; exclusive/open listings are more common teaching focus. Net listings must still meet disclosure and compensation rules.

options.a: Estate from period to period (periodic)
options.b: Estate for years (tenancy for years)
options.c: Tenancy at will (no fixed end date)
options.d: Tenancy at sufferance (holdover)

distractorExplanations.a: A periodic tenancy renews automatically for successive periods and has no definite end date, unlike an estate for years.
distractorExplanations.c: A tenancy at will lasts indefinitely until either party ends it, so it has no definite period.
distractorExplanations.d: A tenancy at sufferance arises when a tenant holds over without consent; it is not a fixed-term estate.

options.a: Close and then file a claim against the Florida Real Estate Recovery Fund
options.b: Pursue contract remedies such as rescission, damages, or specific performance
options.c: Demand that the listing broker cure the title defect at the broker's expense
options.d: Only recover the earnest money; Florida bars damages for title defects

distractorExplanations.a: The Recovery Fund pays for licensee misconduct judgments, not a seller's failure to deliver marketable title.
distractorExplanations.c: Delivering marketable title is the seller's contract duty; the listing broker is not liable to cure title defects.
distractorExplanations.d: Florida does not bar damages; depending on the contract, the buyer may seek rescission, damages, or specific performance.

fl-real-estate-readiness-check-contracts.explanation: Failure to convey marketable title can support buyer remedies under the contract and law. The available remedy depends on the facts and the contract.

options.a: Loan amount divided by appraised value or sale price
options.b: Monthly housing payment divided by gross monthly income
options.c: Total monthly debt divided by gross monthly income
options.d: Down payment divided by appraised value or sale price

distractorExplanations.b: That is the front-end (housing expense) ratio used in underwriting, not loan-to-value.
distractorExplanations.c: That is the back-end debt-to-income ratio, which measures payment capacity rather than leverage.
distractorExplanations.d: Down payment over value is the equity percentage, the complement of LTV, not LTV itself.

fl-real-estate-readiness-check-finance-a.explanation: LTV measures leverage; higher LTV means less borrower equity. Lenders typically use the lower of appraised value and sale price.

options.a: Prepaid interest where 1 point = 1% of the sale price
options.b: Prepaid interest where 1 point = 1% of the loan amount
options.c: A lender fee where 1 point = 1% of the down payment
options.d: Prepaid interest where 1 point lowers the rate by 1%

distractorExplanations.a: A point is calculated on the loan amount, not the sale price; the two differ by the down payment.
distractorExplanations.c: Points are based on the loan amount; the down payment is not the base for any point calculation.
distractorExplanations.d: One point costs 1% of the loan; it typically buys the rate down by only a fraction of a percent, not a full 1%.

options.a: Local property tax millage rates set by counties
options.b: Maximum FHA loan limits set for each county
options.c: Interest rate environments affecting mortgage rates
options.d: Mortgage insurance premiums charged on FHA loans

distractorExplanations.a: Millage rates are set by local taxing authorities, not by Federal Reserve monetary policy.
distractorExplanations.b: FHA loan limits are set by HUD based on area home prices, not by Federal Reserve monetary policy.
distractorExplanations.d: FHA mortgage insurance premiums are set by HUD/FHA, not by the Fed's monetary policy tools.

options.a: Reproduction cost approach
options.b: Income capitalization approach
options.c: Land residual technique
options.d: Sales comparison approach

distractorExplanations.a: The cost approach estimates the cost to build less depreciation plus land value; it does not rely on comparable sales.
distractorExplanations.b: The income approach capitalizes net operating income and is used for income property, not comparable sales.
distractorExplanations.c: The land residual technique is an income-based method that isolates land value, not a comparable sales method.

options.a: Loss in value from outdated design/features
options.b: Loss in value from wear and tear as the building ages
options.c: Loss in value from nearby highway or airport noise
options.d: Loss in value from depreciation of the land over time

distractorExplanations.b: Wear and tear from age is physical deterioration, not functional obsolescence from outdated design.
distractorExplanations.c: Noise from outside the property is external (economic) obsolescence, not a functional design problem.
distractorExplanations.d: Land does not depreciate in appraisal; depreciation applies to improvements, and functional obsolescence is design-related.

fl-real-estate-readiness-check-finance-a.explanation: Functional issues are internal/design; external obsolescence is outside the property; physical is wear. A poor floor plan is a classic example.

options.a: Principal, Interest, Title, and Inspection
options.b: Principal, Interest, Taxes, and Insurance
options.c: Points, Interest, Taxes, and Insurance
options.d: Principal, Income, Taxes, and Inflation

distractorExplanations.a: Title and inspection are closing costs, not monthly payment parts; the T and I are taxes and insurance.
distractorExplanations.c: Points are a one-time closing charge; the P in PITI is principal, the loan balance repayment.
distractorExplanations.d: Income and inflation are not housing payment components; PITI covers interest and insurance.

options.a: Insured by FHA, with mortgage insurance on any down payment
options.b: Guaranteed by the VA for eligible veterans with no down payment
options.c: Not insured/guaranteed by a government agency like FHA/VA
options.d: Funded directly by Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac rather than a lender

distractorExplanations.a: FHA-insured loans are government loans; conventional loans are defined by having no FHA/VA backing.
distractorExplanations.b: A VA guarantee makes the loan a government loan, which is the opposite of conventional financing.
distractorExplanations.d: Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac buy loans in the secondary market; they do not originate conventional loans to borrowers.

fl-real-estate-readiness-check-finance-a.explanation: Conventional loans may use PMI above certain LTVs but aren't FHA/VA government-insured/guaranteed. A conventional loan may still carry private mortgage insurance (PMI).

options.a: Owner-occupied single-family homes in active subdivisions
options.b: Special-purpose buildings such as churches and schools
options.c: Vacant residential lots with recent comparable sales
options.d: Income-producing properties (e.g., rentals, apartments)

distractorExplanations.a: Owner-occupied homes are usually valued by sales comparison because they are bought for use, not income.
distractorExplanations.b: Special-purpose properties with few sales or no income are usually valued by the cost approach.
distractorExplanations.c: Vacant lots with recent sales are usually valued by sales comparison, not by capitalizing income.

options.a: Additional disclosures when certain credit terms are advertised
options.b: Additional disclosures when only the APR is stated in the ad
options.c: A Loan Estimate to be attached to any ad that names a lender
options.d: Lender approval before an ad may state a down payment amount

distractorExplanations.b: The APR alone is not a triggering term; down payment, payment amount, number of payments, or finance charge trigger disclosures.
distractorExplanations.c: A Loan Estimate is given to applicants after an application, not attached to advertising.
distractorExplanations.d: Regulation Z requires extra disclosures when a down payment is advertised, not lender pre-approval of the ad.

fl-real-estate-readiness-check-finance-a.explanation: If ads state down payment, payments, etc., more disclosures are required. The required disclosures include the APR and repayment terms.

options.a: Purchase price minus the original mortgage loan amount
options.b: Market value minus total liens/debt against the property
options.c: Market value minus the original purchase price the owner paid
options.d: Assessed value minus the remaining mortgage balance

distractorExplanations.a: That is only the equity at purchase; equity changes with market value and the current debt balance.
distractorExplanations.c: That is appreciation, not equity; equity subtracts the liens and debt owed against the property.
distractorExplanations.d: Assessed value is for taxation; equity uses market value and all liens, not only the mortgage.

options.a: The rate can change periodically based on the lender's margin, without any caps
options.b: The rate can change periodically based on an index plus margin, subject to caps
options.c: The rate changes only when the borrower refinances into a new loan
options.d: The rate is fixed, but the payment rises on a set schedule each year

distractorExplanations.a: The margin is fixed; the rate moves with the index, and ARMs typically have periodic and lifetime caps.
distractorExplanations.c: Refinancing replaces the loan; an ARM rate adjusts within the same loan on scheduled adjustment dates.
distractorExplanations.d: That describes a graduated payment mortgage, not an adjustable-rate loan tied to an index.

options.a: Loss in value from outdated design or features within the property
options.b: Loss in value from physical wear and tear as the building ages
options.c: Loss in value from external factors such as nearby highway noise
options.d: Loss in value from damage the owner can cure with routine repairs

distractorExplanations.b: Wear and tear from age is physical deterioration, not functional obsolescence from outdated design.
distractorExplanations.c: Factors outside the property cause external (economic) obsolescence, not functional obsolescence.
distractorExplanations.d: Damage cured by repairs is curable physical deterioration, not a design or utility problem inside the property.

options.a: Personal property that has become real property by attachment/intent
options.b: Real property that becomes personal property by severance from land
options.c: Personal property a tenant installs for business and may later remove
options.d: Any movable item listed in the sales contract as included in the sale

distractorExplanations.b: That reverses the concept: severance turns real property into personal property, while a fixture is attached personal property.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes a trade fixture, which stays the tenant's personal property and can be removed before the lease ends.
distractorExplanations.d: Including an item in the contract conveys it but does not make it a fixture; the tests are attachment, adaptation, and intent.

options.a: Taking private property for public use with just compensation
options.b: Zoning, building codes, and land-use regulation for public welfare
options.c: Levying property taxes to fund schools and local services
options.d: Reversion of property to the state when an owner dies without heirs

distractorExplanations.a: That is eminent domain, a separate government power; police power regulates use without payment.
distractorExplanations.c: Taxation is a separate government power over real property, not the police power to regulate land use.
distractorExplanations.d: That is escheat, a different government power; police power covers zoning and building codes.

options.a: Benefits a person or utility company, not a parcel
options.b: Gives revocable permission to enter another's land
options.c: Benefits a dominant estate and runs with the land
options.d: Terminates when the dominant estate is sold

distractorExplanations.a: That describes an easement in gross; an appurtenant easement benefits a dominant parcel of land.
distractorExplanations.b: Revocable permission is a license, which is personal and does not run with the land like an easement.
distractorExplanations.d: An appurtenant easement runs with the land and passes to the buyer of the dominant estate, so a sale does not end it.

options.a: Undivided shares that pass to each owner's heirs by will
options.b: Ownership limited to married couples with survivorship
options.c: Separate ownership of a unit plus shared common elements
options.d: Right of survivorship (and traditionally four unities)

distractorExplanations.a: Shares passing by will to heirs describe tenancy in common; joint tenancy carries a right of survivorship.
distractorExplanations.b: Ownership limited to spouses describes tenancy by the entirety; joint tenancy is open to any co-owners.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes condominium ownership, not a form of co-ownership with survivorship between the owners.

options.a: Upon the death of the measuring life
options.b: Upon the death of the remainderman
options.c: When the life tenant sells the interest
options.d: After a fixed term stated in the deed

distractorExplanations.b: The remainderman's death does not end the life estate; the remainder interest passes to the remainderman's heirs.
distractorExplanations.c: A life tenant can sell the interest, but it continues for the measuring life as a life estate pur autre vie.
distractorExplanations.d: A fixed term describes an estate for years; a life estate is measured by a person's life.

options.a: Single agents must disclose their relationship only after a contract is signed
options.b: Licensees must disclose the type of brokerage relationship as required by law
options.c: Licensees must obtain FREC approval of the relationship before showing property
options.d: Licensees must act as dual agents unless the buyer signs a waiver form

distractorExplanations.a: Florida requires the single agent disclosure before or at the time of entering a listing or showing property, not after contract.
distractorExplanations.c: FREC does not approve individual brokerage relationships; the licensee discloses the relationship type to the customer.
distractorExplanations.d: Dual agency is not allowed in Florida; the choices are single agent, transaction broker, or no brokerage relationship.

options.a: A principal meridian and baseline, then count townships and sections
options.b: A recorded plat, then identify the lot and block within the subdivision
options.c: A point of beginning (POB) and follow courses/distances back to closure
options.d: The assessor's parcel number and follow the tax map boundaries

distractorExplanations.a: Meridians, baselines, townships, and sections belong to the government (rectangular) survey system, not metes and bounds.
distractorExplanations.b: Plat, lot, and block describe the lot-and-block system, which relies on a recorded subdivision map.
distractorExplanations.d: Parcel numbers and tax maps identify land for taxation but are not a legal description method.

options.a: Owner owes no commission if the owner personally finds the buyer during the listing term
options.b: Broker is owed a commission only if the broker or a cooperating agent procures the buyer
options.c: Any broker who brings the buyer earns the fee, and the seller may list with several brokers
options.d: Broker is owed a commission if the property sells during the term regardless of who finds the buyer

distractorExplanations.a: That describes an exclusive agency listing; under exclusive right of sale, the broker is paid even if the owner finds the buyer.
distractorExplanations.b: Procuring-cause payment is the open or exclusive agency idea; exclusive right of sale pays whoever finds the buyer.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes an open listing, where several brokers compete and only the procuring broker is paid.

fl-real-estate-readiness-check-property-.explanation: Exclusive right-of-sale gives the listing broker maximum commission protection; listings need expiration dates. This is the usual term on the typical exclusive right-of-sale form.

options.a: Provide certain creditor and tax assessment benefits for qualifying primary residences
options.b: Provide a full property tax exemption for any Florida residence owned for five years
options.c: Provide creditor and assessment protection for investment rentals and second homes
options.d: Cap annual assessment increases at 10% for primary residences under Save Our Homes

distractorExplanations.b: The homestead exemption reduces assessed value by up to $50,000; it is not a full exemption tied to five years of ownership.
distractorExplanations.c: Homestead protections apply to a qualifying permanent residence, not to rentals or second homes.
distractorExplanations.d: Save Our Homes caps homestead increases at 3% or CPI, whichever is lower; the 10% cap applies to non-homestead property.

fl-real-estate-readiness-check-property-.explanation: Florida homestead has constitutional protections and Save Our Homes assessment concepts—with limits and exceptions (e.g., certain creditors). These benefits are subject to rules and exceptions.

options.a: Directing buyers toward or away from neighborhoods based on protected characteristics
options.b: Denying or limiting financial services in areas based on protected characteristics
options.c: Inducing owners to sell by warning that protected classes are moving in
options.d: Advertising a home in a way that signals a preference for a protected class

distractorExplanations.a: That is steering by licensees, not redlining, which is lenders or insurers denying service in certain areas.
distractorExplanations.c: That describes blockbusting (panic selling), a different prohibited practice from redlining.
distractorExplanations.d: That is discriminatory advertising under the Fair Housing Act, not the area-based lending denial called redlining.

options.a: Return the security deposit within 60 days whether or not a claim is made
options.b: Comply with notice and habitability rules under the Florida Landlord and Tenant Act
options.c: Give a 30-day notice before filing eviction for unpaid rent under Chapter 83
options.d: Allow the tenant to withhold rent for repairs without giving written notice

distractorExplanations.a: Florida requires return within 15 days if no claim is made, or a written claim notice within 30 days; 60 days is not the rule.
distractorExplanations.c: Chapter 83 uses a 3-day notice (excluding weekends and legal holidays) for nonpayment of rent, not 30 days.
distractorExplanations.d: Florida tenants may withhold rent only after a 7-day written notice; the landlord has no duty to accept withholding without notice.

options.a: A listing where the broker's commission is any amount above a seller's net price
options.b: A listing where the broker earns a fixed percentage of the seller's net price
options.c: A listing where the seller pays a flat fee no matter what the sale price is
options.d: A listing where the broker earns a commission only if the broker finds the buyer

distractorExplanations.b: A percentage commission is a standard listing; in a net listing the broker keeps whatever exceeds the seller's net.
distractorExplanations.c: A flat-fee arrangement fixes the broker's pay, while a net listing pays the broker the excess over the net price.
distractorExplanations.d: Paying only when the broker finds the buyer relates to open or exclusive agency listings, not the net price method.

options.a: Testing and abating lead paint before a pre-1978 home can be sold or leased
options.b: Providing required pamphlets/disclosures and opportunity to inspect
options.c: Providing the EPA pamphlet and a 3-day inspection window before closing
options.d: Disclosing known lead hazards only for homes built before 1950

distractorExplanations.a: The federal rule requires disclosure and an inspection opportunity; it does not require testing or abatement before sale.
distractorExplanations.c: Buyers get a 10-day inspection opportunity before they are obligated under the contract, not 3 days before closing.
distractorExplanations.d: The rule covers target housing built before 1978, not only pre-1950 homes.

fl-real-estate-readiness-check-property-.explanation: Federal lead disclosure rules apply to most pre-1978 residential target housing. This must happen before the buyer or tenant is obligated under the contract or lease.
